characters.name: Habakkuk

genealogy.note: Habakkuk 1:1 and 3:1 name him only as 'Habakkuk the prophet'; the book supplies no father, tribe, hometown, or family details at all.

verses.note: Superscription: 'The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see' — introduces the whole book as a vision received by the prophet.

Habakkuk's first complaint to the LORD: he cries out over violence and 'spoiling' with no answer; 'the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth,' because 'the wicked doth compass about the righteous.'
Habakkuk's second complaint: appeals to the LORD's everlasting holiness and asks how a God 'of purer eyes than to behold evil' can look on the treachery of the instrument he has raised up.
'I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me' — Habakkuk positions himself to wait for the LORD's reply.
Commanded to 'write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it,' with assurance that though it tarry, 'it will surely come, it will not tarry.'
Superscription of his closing psalm: 'A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth' — a musical/poetic term of uncertain meaning.
His physical reaction to the vision of the LORD's coming: 'my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones.'

His closing resolution of faith: even if the fig tree does not blossom and 'there shall be no herd in the stalls,' 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation'; closes 'To the chief singer on my stringed instruments,' marking it for musical/liturgical use.

funFacts: Called only 'Habakkuk the prophet' (1:1, 3:1) — the text gives no father's name, hometown, or tribe, unlike several other Minor Prophets.
One of the few prophetic books built mainly as a dialogue/complaint between the prophet and the LORD, rather than a series of oracles delivered to the people.
'Shigionoth' (3:1) and the three 'Selah' markers within his closing prayer (3:3, 3:9, 3:13) are musical/liturgical notations also found in the Psalms.

characters.name: The Chaldeans — Raised Up for Judgment
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, in direct answer to Habakkuk's first complaint (1:5-11)
characters.purpose: Answers Habakkuk's complaint that 'wrong judgment proceedeth' (1:4) by announcing a coming work 'which ye will not believe, though it be told you' (1:5): the LORD is raising up 'the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation' (1:6) to march through the land and seize dwellingplaces not their own. Their swiftness, violence, and self-glorifying strength ('imputing this his power unto his god,' 1:11) are described at length, but the text names their coming victims only obliquely — as 'the land' (1:6), 'they' (1:9-10), and, in Habakkuk's own follow-up complaint, 'us' and 'the righteous' (1:4,1:12-13) — never as Judah or any other specific nation.

verses.note: 'Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days, which ye will not believe, though it be told you.'

'I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, which shall march through the breadth of the land, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs. They are terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves.'
Their horses are 'swifter than the leopards,' 'more fierce than the evening wolves,' and their horsemen 'fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat.'
They come 'for violence,' gather captives 'as the sand,' scoff at kings and princes, and 'deride every strong hold' by heaping dust and taking it.
'Then shall his mind change, and he shall pass over, and offend, imputing this his power unto his god' — the Chaldean power credits its own conquests to its own god.

Habakkuk likens the Chaldean's conquest to a fisherman: he 'taketh up all of them with the angle,' catches them in his net, 'rejoiceth' and 'sacrificeth unto his net,' emptying it 'and not spare continually to slay the nations.'

funFacts: The word 'Chaldeans' (1:6) is the only name the book gives this power — the more familiar name 'Babylon' never actually appears anywhere in the book of Habakkuk.
The Chaldean's underlying flaw is diagnosed at the start of the next tier's material (2:4-5): a soul 'lifted up' that 'enlargeth his desire as hell... and cannot be satisfied.'

characters.name: The Just Shall Live by Faith
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, as the heart of his written answer to Habakkuk (2:2-4)
characters.purpose: Introduced immediately after the command to 'write the vision, and make it plain upon tables' (2:2) and the assurance that the vision, though it tarry, 'will surely come' (2:3): sets a proud, self-inflated soul ('his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him,' 2:4a) against 'the just,' who 'shall live by his faith' (2:4b) — the verse on which Habakkuk's own movement from complaint to trust turns.

verses.note: 'Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it... though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.'
'Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.'

funFacts: Positioned as the hinge between the LORD's description of the proud, insatiable oppressor (2:4a, continued in 2:5) and the five woes that follow (2:6-20).

characters.name: The Five Woes
characters.deliveredBy: Habakkuk, voicing a 'parable' and 'taunting proverb' (2:6) placed in the mouths of the plundered peoples ('shall not all these take up a parable against him... and say,' 2:6) against the same proud, insatiable power described in 2:5
characters.purpose: A series of five funeral-style 'woe' oracles (2:6-20) condemning the oppressor for unjust gain (2:6-8), house-building on 'evil covetousness' (2:9-11), founding a city on bloodshed (2:12-14), degrading a neighbor with drink (2:15-17), and trusting in dumb, breathless idols (2:18-20). The oppressor's victims are named only as 'many nations' and 'all that dwell therein' (2:8,17) — the book never names a specific victim nation such as Judah anywhere in this cycle or elsewhere.

verses.note: Woe 1: 'Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his!... shall not thy creditors rise up'; 'because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee.'
Woe 2: 'Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high'; 'the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.'

Woe 3: 'Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity!' — answered by the promise that 'the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.'
Woe 4: 'Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink... that thou mayest look on their nakedness!' — his own shame and the 'cup of the LORD's right hand' shall be turned back upon him.

Woe 5, against idolatry: 'Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach!... there is no breath at all in the midst of it. But the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him.'

funFacts: 2:14 ('the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea') is one of the book's best-known single verses, embedded inside the third woe rather than standing alone.
2:20 ('the LORD is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him') closes the woe-cycle by contrasting the living LORD with the silent, breathless idols just condemned.
The five woes never repeat the name 'Chaldeans' — they continue addressing 'him' (singular) as introduced in 2:5, the same proud, insatiable power described in chapter 1.

characters.name: Habakkuk's Prayer — the LORD's Coming
characters.deliveredBy: Habakkuk, in a prayer/psalm addressed to the LORD (3:1-19)
characters.purpose: Habakkuk's closing prayer 'upon Shigionoth' (3:1), recalling the LORD's dramatic coming — 'God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran' (3:3) — marching through the earth amid cosmic upheaval (trembling mountains, standing sun and moon, subdued sea and rivers) 'for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed' (3:13). It moves from Habakkuk's own trembling fear at the vision (3:16) to his closing resolution to rejoice in the LORD regardless of circumstance (3:17-19).

verses.note: 'O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid... in wrath remember mercy.'
'God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.'

'I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble' — Cushan and Midian are named only as trembling witnesses to the LORD's approach, with no further action given to either.
'The mountains saw thee, and they trembled... the sun and moon stood still in their habitation.'
'Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked.'

Habakkuk's closing resolution: though 'the fig tree shall not blossom' and 'there shall be no herd in the stalls,' 'yet I will rejoice in the LORD'; closes 'To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.'

funFacts: Contains three 'Selah' markers (3:3, 3:9, 3:13), a musical/liturgical pause notation shared with many Psalms.
'Teman' and 'mount Paran' (3:3) are locations associated with Edom/Sinai; the prayer states only that the LORD 'came' from those places — it does not itself name the Exodus or Sinai.
Cushan and Midian (3:7) appear only as place-names reacting in fear to the LORD's approach — neither is given any further role anywhere in the book.

notes:
Habakkuk is a 3-chapter, 56-verse Minor Prophet structured as a dialogue between the prophet and the LORD (chapters 1-2) followed by Habakkuk's own theophanic prayer/psalm (chapter 3). Given its small scope, this index uses five scribe tiers rather than a narrative book's larger person-heavy roster: one person-tier for Habakkuk himself, and four law/theme-tiers for the book's major oracular content.

Two accuracy points are load-bearing for this redraft (the first corrects the prior draft's flagged error):
1. The book never names the nation whose sin prompts Habakkuk's opening complaint, nor the nation victimized by the Chaldeans in the woe-cycle — it is called only 'the land,' 'us,' 'the righteous,' 'many nations,' and 'all that dwell therein' (1:2-4, 1:12-13, 2:8, 2:17). No tier or entry in this index asserts 'Judah' or any other specific victim nation.
2. The book never uses the word 'Babylon.' The oppressing power is named only 'the Chaldeans' (1:6, the sole occurrence), which this index preserves throughout (tier names, purpose fields, funFacts) rather than substituting the more familiar but textually absent 'Babylon.'

No submanagers were used: Cushan and Midian (3:7) are place-names that tremble at the LORD's approach but take no narrative action, so they are handled as citations within the theophany_prayer entry and in the top-level genealogyLists rather than as standalone submanager entries.
